column1: What mathematical structure encodes both rotation and translation in a single compact representation for robotic pose transformations?
column2: A homogeneous transformation matrix in SE(3), a 4×4 matrix combining a rotation matrix R in SO(3) with a translation vector t, enabling pose transformation via simple matrix multiplication.

column1: Why does Euler angle sequencing (e.g., yaw-pitch-roll vs pitch-yaw-roll) produce different final orientations for the same initial pose?
column2: Because rotations do not commute in SO(3); the order of rotation application changes the final orientation, and this non-commutativity can cause gimbal lock singularities that destabilize naive control algorithms.

What happens when master haptic forces are directly coupled to slave robot forces across network delay in bilateral teleoperation?

column1: What is the passivity constraint in bilateral teleoperator design?
column2: The two-port network model of the teleoperator must not generate energy over time, regardless of operator manipulation or environmental disturbance forces—expressible via scattering theory or positive-real transfer function constraints.

column1: What are typical round-trip network latencies for LAN, continental, and satellite teleoperation links?
column2: ~20 ms for LAN, ~100 ms for continental distances, ~250 ms for satellite links.

column1: What historical origin gave rise to bilateral control theory in teleoperation?
column2: The nuclear industry's need in the 1950s to manipulate radioactive materials behind lead shielding using mechanical master-slave manipulators, later transitioning to electrical transmission which introduced delay.

column1: What is the core fidelity principle that resolves the sim-to-real transfer problem in robot learning, avoiding the need for molecular-level simulation?
column2: Task-relevant fidelity: simulators need only reproduce the minimal set of physical phenomena (e.g., contact dynamics, mass distribution, visual variation) that dominate task performance, discarding irrelevant details for computational tractability.

column1: What practical constraints make physical-hardware-only reinforcement learning for robot manipulation economically prohibitive?
column2: Actuator wear limits training to thousands of episodes, human supervision costs scale linearly with training time, and catastrophic exploration failures destroy expensive hardware—potentially requiring six months and multiple robot replacements for a single policy.

column1: What sampling rate ranges characterize vision systems, IMUs, microphone arrays, and eye-tracking in multimodal HRI sensor fusion?
column2: Vision: 30–90 Hz (occlusion/lighting issues); IMUs: 200–1000 Hz (excellent temporal resolution but drift); Microphones: 16–48 kHz; Eye-tracking: 60–250 Hz (predicts intent 200–500 ms before motion).

column1: In real-time gesture recognition for robotics, what is the core sequential decision tradeoff at each timestep?
column2: Whether to emit a gesture classification immediately (risking premature/incorrect robot behavior) or wait for more evidence (risking excessive latency and unresponsiveness).
